subject: DSM - model building, soap film, multicollinearity, grid cell size

messages.author: 3c8299ac8234f5d2
messages.subject: DSM - model building, soap film, multicollinearity, grid cell size
parts:
Dear listfolk,

I am building a DSM for coastal cetaceans occurring in a small embayment (400-500 sq. km) and I have several questions, some technical, some a bit more philosophical. Apologies for the number of queries; I thought it best to combine them rather than write individual posts.

I have been working off the very thorough vignettes on pantropical dolphins and common loons found at https://github.com/dill/dsm/wiki/Examples. I am using R 3.1.1 and the latest version of packages dsm and Distance.

Q1. As with many biological datasets of elusive, intermittenly available species, many of my segments are associated with zero counts. What is the best way to deal with zero-inflation in a DSM context?

I have tried using a negative binomial and a Tweedie distribution. Both are obvious improvements over Poisson (from inspecting the residuals) yet my best model thus far only explains about 6% of the deviance (see residual plot attached) and most candidate models tested returned smaller (or sometimes negative!) %Dev. I am therefore wondering whether negbin and Tweedie are appropriate at all and whether I should explore alternative distributions such as those found in the gamlss package (e.g. zero-adjusted/inflated Poisson)?

Q2. What is the rationale behind the choice of maximum basis sizes in gams? In the common loon example, these are set to 10 for univariate smooths and 18 for bivariate smooths. Is this simply a judgement call?

Q3. Is multicollinearity (concurvity?) something to worry about in a DSM? It appears that neither the dolphin nor the loon examples investigate covariate relationships (e.g. via variance inflation factors) prior to model fitting. Is this because the particular gam formulation used is not sensitive to collinearity, or any other reason I may have missed?

Q4. I am trying to gain a sense for whether a soap film smoother would be justified in my case - my study area is in my view fairly complex (it includes mangrove areas, small river mouths etc.) and we know that cetaceans do not occur onshore so a soap film that reduces edge effects would appear sensible. In the common loon example however, no soap films were used despite the study area encompassing Rhode Island. Is there a reason why a soap film was not considered in that study? I would have thought regular smoothers would be prone to smoothing over the island. 

Also, when a soap film is being used, are there any general guidelines on how to choose the number of knots in the make.soapgrid command? The soaps I have tried generally tend to produce much larger abundance estimates, mostly due to a single isolated "hotspot" of predicted abundance in a corner of the studya area away from where the majority of sightings have been made.

Q5. I calculated the size of my prediction grid cells in GIS but I would like to make sure I haven't missed anything obvious. The reason I ask is that in this recent post, Dave and Eric explained that cell sizes (444 sq km) could be obtained in GIS or from the width/height attributes of the cells in R.

However, in the Mexico dolphins example the grid cell centroids are situated approx.16 km apart (according to my GIS). This would correspond to a grid cell area of 16x16=256 sq km, not 444 sq km. This also contrasts with the height and width of preddata in R (32.072 and 37.065 km respectively) which give an area of 32.072 x 37.065 = 1189 sq km, again not 444 sq km ... so I am slightly confused. How was the value of 444 sqkm obtained?

Q6. Finally in Winiarski et al. (2013), the paper which accompanies the common loon example, the best detection function model (under AIC) was a hazard rate without covariates. The associated DSM thus used N as the response variable, but the equation on page 277 shows Nhat. Shouldn't this equation have shown N with an offset reflecting the effective area of the segment (calculated based on the estimated effective strip width) instead? What should one report in a paper when using density/abundance as the response?

Many thanks in advance for any thoughts/wisdom/advice anyone is willing to share.
Phil

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] DSM - model building, soap film, multicollinearity, grid cell size
parts:
Hi Phil, hi listfolk,

I'm sure that most of them are certainly pertinent to folks on this list
engaged in building DSMs... I'll try to answer as much as I can, but
others should certainly chime in with their experiences


Q1. Zero-inflation: Worth considering here whether the model is truly
zero-inflated vs. just having many zeros. True zero-inflation would mean
too many zeros conditional on the model (as opposed to many in the
data). There are a few techniques to test this (though I don't have
personal experience of them): Broek (1995) and Yang, Hardin and Addy
(2010) (courtesy of Ben Bolker on StackOverflow).

I assume you're using nb() for the negative binomial response, so the
parameter is estimated at the same time as the other parameters (this is
much much faster than the old negbin() response). If that's not working
AND you have true zero-inflation AND you have count (as opposed to
estimated count/abundance) you could use the new ziplss() response which
implements a zero-inflated Poisson model (you may need to update mgcv
using update.packages() in R).

For what it's worth, I think your residual plots look okay. You may want
to use the dsm::rqgam.check() function to see if there is any real
structure in the resids vs fitted plot (see this slide
http://converged.yt/talks/duke-dsm/talk.html#%2850%29 and Dunn and Smyth
(1996) for more about randomised quantile residuals).


Q2. Basis size: This is a topic of some controversy as many folks think
that the size should be limited to allow for "realistic" covariate
effects (e.g. that if the resulting smooths are too wiggly this is not
very realistic). I have been more an advocate of letting the data tell
you what it can and although the resulting smooths may be wiggly on a
small scale, the broad trends are what we're interested in. There is
advice on choosing basis size in line with the latter philosophy in the
mgcv help page ?choose.k.

Q3. Concurvity: I haven't spent enough time really grappling with this
issue directly yet. What I have experienced is that there are
differences in which smooths are selected in the model, depending on
which of a series of covariates are removed first (or which are included
in the first place). This problem is less pronounced when using
method="REML" in my experience. (This is mainly folk story territory for
me at the moment.)

I did find the other day that mgcv has a function called concurvity()
that will estimate the concurvity between your smooths, this probably
bears more investigation.


Q4. Soap: We didn't use the soap film for the Rhode Island analysis
mainly due to a time constraint on our part. But I also note that there
wasn't evidence of leakage through the island in the resulting models
(e.g. see plots in
https://github.com/dill/MEPS-analysis/blob/master/MEPS-analysis.pdf).

Soap films can be tricky and frustrating to setup and fit, you may find
a script I wrote to check your knot setup useful:
https://github.com/dill/soap_checker I don't know about general
guidelines. I've had success in evenly spaced knots across the study
area, but the number of knots depends on the complexity of the spatial
component of the model. You may also need to increase the basis size of
the cyclic boundary smooth, via the k= argument.


Q5. Mexico data: This is a really good question and I'm embarrassed that
I'd not noticed this before. As far as I know the areas were calculated
by GIS before the data (originally form NOAA) was imported into a
Distance (for Windows) project. I then extracted the data from that
project and I had assumed that the data coming in from Distance were
correct. I will check this out and report back to the list. Thanks for
noticing this!!


Q6. Response: Both Nhat and N (i.e. estimated abundance per segment and
count per segment) can be used when no covariates are included in the
detection function (as can N be used when covariates are used, provided
that the covariates only vary at the scale of the segment).

BUT in this case for the final model it looks like we did use N (see the
MEPS-analysis.pdf linked above) though for the majority of the models we
used Nhat. I can't remember why we did this (maybe to de-complicate the
stats part of the paper, maybe space constraint), but I agree this is
misleading.

In general I would not do what we did and instead report exactly the
model used.


Hope this begins to clear up some of those questions, do ask for
elaboration on any of the above if that's useful.


All the best,
--dave


---

References


Broek, Jan van den. 1995. A Score Test for Zero Inflation in a Poisson
Distribution. Biometrics 51 (2): 738–43. doi:10.2307/2532959.

Dunn, PK, and GK Smyth. Randomized Quantile Residuals. Journal of
Computational and Graphical Statistics 5, no. 3 (1996): 236–244.

Yang, Zhao, James W. Hardin, and Cheryl L. Addy. 2010. “Score Tests for
Zero-Inflation in Overdispersed Count Data.” Communications in
Statistics - Theory and Methods 39 (11): 2008–30.
doi:10.1080/03610920902948228./03610920902948228#.VDVM81QUBAs
